candidates.title: Differential active adhesion and a capillary instability drive global eversion and dissemination of bacterial colonies
candidates.authors: Stephan Wimmi, Isabelle Wielert, Kai Zhou, Marc Hennes, Benedikt Sabass, Berenike Maier
candidates.abstract: Abstract Attractive forces between cells can determine the shape and sorting behaviour of bacterial colonies. During colony development, chemical gradients form within the colony, but it is unclear how they affect cohesion. Here we discover that such gradients trigger global eversion of proliferating colonies formed by the human pathogen Neisseria gonorrhoeae . Like a jet, the inner core flows towards the periphery where it is partially dispersed and partially spreads around the core of the colony. Living dispersed cells reform colonies, leading to rapid dissemination. The eversion depends on local oxygen depletion, which reduces the activity of the molecular motors that govern self-attraction: before the eversion, the colony consists of a weakly cohesive spherical core surrounded by a strongly cohesive shell. An idealized computational model reveals that, in this configuration, an instability analogous to a capillary instability emerges when the thickness of the strongly interacting shell falls below a critical value. We show that the probability for eversion strongly depends on the motor-generated attractive force between bacteria. Overall, our results indicate that chemical gradients induce spontaneous symmetry breaking in a mechanically active colony, thereby triggering a nonlinear shape instability. This instability generates large-scale cellular fluxes that redistribute bacteria towards environments more favourable for their growth.

candidates.title: Transcriptional nodes governing diversity and effector rewiring of a plastic liver invariant natural killer T cell ecosystem
candidates.authors: Jun Yamanouchi, Josep Garnica, Enric Canut, Shari Thiessen, Thomas Papp-Simon, Joel Moro, Debajyoti Mondal, Pau Serra, Pere Santamaria
candidates.abstract: Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are thought to exit the thymus as terminally differentiated subsets that seed tissues with fixed effector biases. However, the composition, regulatory architecture and plasticity of tissue-resident iNKT cell compartments remain ill-defined. Here, we chart the cellular diversity and transcription-factor (TF) circuitry of mouse liver-resident iNKT (LiNKT) cells and delineate intrahepatic differentiation at steady state and following repeated intravascular αGalCer/CD1d stimulation. Single-cell profiling identifies eight subsets with distinct transcriptional signatures—LiNKT2 (IL-4/IL-13-biased), LiNKT17 (IL-17A-biased), LiNKTR1 (TR1-like, IL-10-biased), and five NKT1-like (IFNγ-biased) states including LiNKT1.1, LiNKT1.2, LiNKT1.3, Klrg1lowCx3cr1low Effector and Klrg1highCx3cr1high Effector populations. Trajectory and compositional analyses reveal that iterative stimulation expands LiNKT2 and drives their conversion into LiNKTR1, while LiNKT1.1 seeds Effector and Klrg1⁺Cx3cr1⁺ Effector states, revealing local specification layered atop thymic priming. Conditional deletion across seven signature TFs associated with each subset maps subset dependencies and fate transitions: BCL-6 and TCF-1 sustain global iNKT output and, together with T-BET, license all NKT1-like states. BCL-6, ID3, and IRF4 drive Effector LiNKT1; BCL-6 and c-MAF specify LiNKT17; BLIMP-1 promotes LiNKT2 and, with c-MAF and IRF4, enforces LiNKTR1 specification. BLIMP-1 and ID3 oppose each other in LiNKTR1 versus Effector LiNKT1 differentiation. Thus, the hepatic iNKT compartment emerges as a TF-wired, plastic network in which local cues and subset-specific TF combinations govern lineage progression, nominating actionable nodes for tuning liver inflammation and repair. The transcriptional diversity of liver-resident invariant natural killer T (LiNKT) cells remains incompletely understood. Here, the authors map eight mouse LiNKT cell subsets and show how transcription factors guide their conversion into inflammatory or regulatory states, revealing targets for controlling liver inflammation and repair.

candidates.title: Rigidity-driven molecular assembly for high-efficiency flexible perovskite/CIGS tandems
candidates.authors: Libing Yao, Enbing Bi, Qingqing Liu, Ke Zhao, Caner Değer, Ilhan Yavuz, Jingjing Zhou, Weizhong Tian, Xiaohe Miao, Jiahui Shen, Yang Gui, Yixin Luo, Jiazhe Xu, Xu Zhang, Tie Guo, Jingjing Xue, Rui Wang
candidates.abstract: Monolithic flexible perovskite/Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS) tandem solar cells (TSCs) are pivotal for next-generation flexible photovoltaics, owing to their high power-to-weight ratio and mechanical compliance. However, their development is constrained by the challenge of depositing high-quality hole-selective contacts (HSCs) onto intrinsically rough CIGS bottom cells. Conventional molecular interlayers often exhibit poor packing on such surfaces, leading to interfacial defects that compromise both efficiency and stability. Here, we report Py6, a rigid molecule engineered with an enforced vinylene (C = C) bridge to ensure molecular planarity and extended π-conjugation. This structural rigidity fosters a highly ordered nanoscale assembly that effectively templates the growth of dense, void-free perovskite layers while optimizing interfacial energetic alignment. Consequently, our champion flexible TSC achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 28.21% (0.0749 cm2, certified 27.58%), while large-area devices (1.010 cm2) reached 25.63%, with a certified PCE of 25.19% and a certified stabilized PCE of 25.16%. Furthermore, the resulting devices exhibit exceptional durability, retaining 93.8% of their initial PCE after 400 hours of continuous 1-sun operation and 94.2% after 5000 rigorous bending cycles. Our rigidity-driven molecular design overcomes the critical interfacial bottlenecks of non-planar photovoltaics, providing a robust pathway for high-performance, mechanically resilient flexible tandem technologies. Flexible perovskite and copper indium gallium selenide tandem solar cells are hindered by rough interfaces that reduce efficiency and stability. Yao et al. designed a rigid molecular contact enabling efficient, durable devices that withstand prolonged operation and bending.

candidates.title: Identification and functional characterization of bacterial bilirubin vinyl reductase across vertebrate gut microbiomes
candidates.authors: Angela K. Jiang, Maggie R. Grant, Gabriela Arp, Keith Dufault-Thompson, Alexandra M. Clarke, Yue Li, Danielle Lehman, Alan K. Jarmusch, Brantley Hall, Xiaofang Jiang
candidates.abstract: Abstract Gut bacteria reduce bilirubin to urobilinogen, allowing it to be excreted through feces and urine, but studies have long noted a heterogeneous mixture of partially reduced bilirubin-derived intermediates, suggesting that multiple enzymes are involved. Here we identify bilirubin vinyl reductase (BilV), an Old Yellow Enzyme family reductase encoded in the genomic neighborhood of the known bilirubin reductase ( bilR ). Using heterologous expression and LC–MS/MS, we show that BilR acts on the methine bridges in the bilirubin reduction pathway; co-expression with BilV enables vinyl-group reduction and complete conversion to urobilinogen. In bacterial genomes, bilV co-occurs primarily with the bilR -insertion subtype and is largely absent alongside bilR -short. Analysis of 1,197 gut metagenomes across 14 vertebrate species reveals that this differential co-occurrence shapes pathway availability across hosts: carnivores and omnivores carry balanced bilR and bilV , whereas avian microbiomes, dominated by bilR -short, are depleted for bilV . These findings establish that bilirubin reduction to urobilinogen involves two enzymes with complementary regioselectivity, revising the previous model, and that their distribution across vertebrate gut microbiomes varies in relation to host bile pigment chemistry.

candidates.title: A membrane-active cationic supramolecule to treat both fungal and bacterial keratitis
candidates.authors: Adrielle Xianwen Chen, Thet Tun Aung, Tianjiao Dai, Eve Wai Ling Chow, Jianguo Li, Keefe Oei, Venkatesh Mayandi, Sai Bo Bo Tun, Amutha Veluchamy Barathi, Darren Shu Jeng Ting, Yi Yan Yang, Chandra Shekhar Verma, Rajamani Lakshminarayanan, Yue Wang, Ning Li
candidates.abstract: Rising antimicrobial resistance (AMR) underscores the urgent need for new antimicrobial strategies. We report here a membrane-active cationic supramolecule and its strong therapeutic efficacy against both fungal and bacterial keratitis in animal models. The lead Y8 design displayed broad-spectrum activity against various fungal pathogens, with low-µM MIC90, rapid action kinetics, and resistance evasion. Mechanistically, it disrupts the fungal cytoplasmic membrane and interacts with the cell wall glucan. Y8 is ocular compatible and, more importantly, shows higher/comparable efficacy to voriconazole, natamycin and amphotericin B in treating Candida, Fusarium and Aspergillus keratitis in mice or rabbits, respectively. It further displays strong activity against pathogenic bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), with markedly better treatment outcomes than vancomycin in a mouse MRSA keratitis model. Overall, here we demonstrate a safe, potent, and cross-kingdom antimicrobial strategy, which may potentially contribute to the frontline infection management and AMR crisis mitigation. In this work, authors report a membrane-active cationic supramolecule, Y8, with potent cross-kingdom activity against vision-threatening fungal and bacterial keratitis. It is ocular-compatible and outperforms or matches standard therapies in animal models.

candidates.title: Anyone can be the best depending on how structural variant callers are evaluated
candidates.authors: Luca Denti, Thomas Krannich, Tomas Vinar, Rayan Chikhi, Paola Bonizzoni, Brona Brejova, Fereydoun Hormozdiari
candidates.abstract: Abstract Structural variants (SVs) are medium- and large-scale genomic alterations that shape phenotypic diversity and disease risk. Numerous methods have been proposed for discovering SVs, however their benchmarking has been inconsistent across studies, often resulting in contradictory findings. We evaluate the performance of several SV discovery methods for detecting unbalanced SVs from long-read sequencing data and observe substantial variation in performance and ranking depending on the choice of ground truth, reference genome, and genomic regions used for evaluation. Our results indicate that these discrepancies largely arise from inconsistencies among SV callsets used as ground truth, ranging from consortium-curated benchmarks to callsets derived from high-quality assemblies. These discrepancies call for additional caution in downstream analyses and in drawing conclusions based on predicted SVs. Our findings underscore the complexity of evaluating SV detection methods and highlight the need for careful consideration and field-standard practices when reporting performance metrics.

candidates.title: Buried stochastic interfaces enabling depth-multiplexed optical physical unclonable functions
candidates.authors: Taeyeong Kim, Kibum Jung, Jungchul Lee
candidates.abstract: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) convert irreproducible physical disorder into device-unique responses for hardware authentication. However, many optical PUFs rely on surface- or near-surface-accessible features, coupling optical readability to vulnerability to inspection, replication, and data-driven inference. Here we introduce optically hidden silicon PUFs that encode physically protected entropy at buried membrane–cavity interfaces and enable its readout through depth-selective optical gating. Annealing of high-aspect-ratio hole arrays produces multilayer silicon architectures with device-specific buried interfacial roughness concealed beneath a planarized, optically featureless surface. Spectro-angular- and polarization-selective illumination enables deterministic readout across eight buried interfaces in the primary configuration. The responses exhibit an inter-device Hamming distance of 0.5011 ± 0.0060 (mean ± s.d.), depth-plane discrimination accuracies of 98.9−99.4%, and 0.080% generated-response acceptance under a challenge-held-out best-of-Ksearch = 64 spoofing evaluation at a fixed impostor false-positive rate of 10−3. Redundancy-aware depth multiplexing yields a pairwise-redundancy-screened, spatial-predictability-adjusted effective pre-ECC response budget of ~0.74×108 bits per 200×200μm2 pattern while retaining wafer-scale manufacturability. These results establish buried-interface depth multiplexing as a scalable route to physically protected optical authentication. Optical physical unclonable functions often rely on surface-accessible features. Here, the authors conceal stochastic nanotexture at vertically stacked silicon interfaces beneath a planarized surface and use depth-selective optical gating to read eight planes for reliable hardware authentication.

candidates.title: Control of out-of-plane anti-damping spin torque with a canted ferromagnetic spin source
candidates.authors: Xiaoxi Huang, Daniel A. Pharis, Hang Zhou, Zishen Tian, Thow Min Jerald Cham, Zhaoyang Wang, Yuhan Liang, Kyoungjun Lee, Yilin Evan Li, Maciej Olszewski, Di Yi, Chang-Beom Eom, Darrell G. Schlom, Lane W. Martin, Ding-Fu Shao, Daniel C. Ralph
candidates.abstract: To achieve efficient anti-damping switching of nanoscale magnetic memories with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy using spin-orbit torque requires that the anti-damping spin-orbit torque have a strong out-of-plane component. The spin anomalous Hall effect and the planar Hall effect spin current produced by a ferromagnetic layer are candidate mechanisms for producing such an out-of-plane anti-damping torque, but both require that the magnetic moment of the spin source layer be canted partly out of the sample plane at zero applied magnetic field. Here we demonstrate such a canted configuration for a ferromagnetic SrRuO3 layer, and we characterize all vector components of the torque that it produces, including non-zero out-of-plane anti-damping torques. We verify that the out-of-plane spin component can be tuned by the orientation of the magnetic moment, with significant contributions from both the spin anomalous Hall effect and the planar Hall effect spin current. Huang et al. show that canted magnetization in SrRuO3 generates a sizable out-of-plane damping-like torque without relying on low crystal symmetry, offering a strategy toward scalable magnetic-memory devices with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy.

candidates.title: Expanding antimicrobial chemical space by engineering drug safety
candidates.authors: Tahoura Samad, Chayanon Ngambenjawong, Henry Ko, Savan Patel, Cristiana DeAgazio, Heather E. Fleming, Sangeeta N. Bhatia
candidates.abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) infections are a major health threat. Although advances in high-throughput screening, genome mining, and machine learning have accelerated antimicrobial discovery, insufficient separation between antibacterial efficacy and host toxicity remains a bottleneck to the clinical development of new antimicrobial compounds. Here, we establish a generalizable, two-component strategy to engineer drug safety and mobilize otherwise inaccessible chemical space for antimicrobial therapy, using calicheamicin, a potent cytotoxin with unacceptable host toxicity, as a proof of concept. First, we engineer a conditionally active drug conjugate that limits calicheamicin activity to infected tissue, thereby reducing systemic toxicity. Second, we engineer a self-resistance enzyme from Micromonospora echinospora , the natural producer of calicheamicin, as a long-circulating antidote to neutralize calicheamicin outside infected tissue, further reducing off-target toxicity. The conjugate exhibits activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens upon exposure to a protease present within the infected microenvironment. When delivered with the antidote, antibacterial efficacy is maintained while off-target toxicity is reduced in mouse models of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial pneumonia. We anticipate that our dual strategy, which engineers drug safety rather than selecting for it, provides a generalizable framework for mobilizing promising but toxic compounds as antimicrobials.

candidates.title: Changing mercury exposure in the Yukon Watershed linked to traditional diet shifts and permafrost thaw
candidates.authors: M. Isabel Smith, Emily A. Seelen, Edda A. Mutter, Anna R. Godduhn, Marie E. Lowe, John S. Magyar, A. Joshua West
candidates.abstract: Abstract Rapid Arctic warming is disrupting ecosystems and traditional subsistence resources, and simultaneously may release toxic mercury into aquatic ecosystems. Together, these changes threaten food security and public health. In the Yukon River Basin of Alaska, many Indigenous communities that traditionally rely on subsistence fishing are facing precipitous declines in salmon populations. Alternative protein sources can contain up to eight times more mercury, with burbot, northern pike, and beluga being major dietary mercury contributors. More reliance on these proteins could increase mercury exposure, while permafrost thaw is projected to increase mercury concentrations in fish by 21–175% by 2100. Here, we combine diet surveys and subsistence harvest data to develop a hypothetical dietary mercury model. Dietary shifts and permafrost-driven increases in fish mercury could increase mercury intake up to 486%, potentially exceeding public health guidelines and highlighting the vulnerability of Arctic food systems to interacting environmental and ecological change.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Humans infer the nutrient content of foods from sensory cues, yet the neural and computational basis of these inferences remains unclear. Here we show how oral texture contributes to judgements of fat content by combining purpose-designed foods that dissociated fat from texture with behavioural testing, computational modelling, functional neuroimaging during consumption, and a naturalistic feeding assay. Judgements of fat content reflected established relationships between oral texture and fat and became systematically less accurate when these relationships were violated. A computational model formalized these failures as prediction errors—discrepancies between fat content predicted from texture and actual fat content. During food consumption, the hypothalamus encoded these model-derived prediction errors, responding most strongly when texture predicted more fat than the food contained. Individual differences in hypothalamic sensitivity to texture predicted fat intake during an ad libitum meal. These findings show how sensory inference of fat content engages hypothalamic signals predicting food intake.

candidates.title: Molecular basis for thermoresponsive protein condensation in plants
candidates.authors: Sunita Pathak, Ananya Chakravarti, Carissa Bersche, David A. Korasick, Yuren Cao, Jerelle A. Joseph, Lucia C. Strader
candidates.abstract: Plants continuously experience temperature fluctuations that shape their physiology, development, and survival. Yet, how plants sense and adapt to elevated temperatures at the molecular level remains only partially understood. Here, we uncover a sequence-encoded mechanism by which plant proteins directly sense temperature through condensation. Focusing on prion-like low-complexity domains (PLCDs) in Arabidopsis thaliana, we combine cellular imaging, quantitative biophysics, and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to show that numerous PLCDs undergo reversible lower critical solution temperature (LCST)-type phase transitions. We find that PLCDs that are sufficient and necessary for condensation confer thermoresponsive variability to full-length proteins. Sequence analysis and simulations reveal that thermoresponsiveness is encoded in compositional heuristics, with sufficient PLCDs enriched in aliphatic and aromatic residues, enabling accurate prediction and rational tuning of condensation thresholds. Engineered variants with altered sequence composition exhibit predictable shifts in thermoresponsive condensation, confirming a direct, sequence-level encoding of temperature sensitivity. Our findings establish LCST-driven phase transitions as common amongst plant PLCD-containing proteins and provide a molecular framework for designing synthetic biomolecules with programmable temperature responses. Molecular temperature sensing is not fully understood. Here, the authors show that many Arabidopsis prion-like low-complexity domain-containing proteins undergo phase transitions which might act as temperature sensors.

Here, we report dual-comb photoacoustic Brillouin spectroscopy for scan-free measurement within the dual-comb bandwidth and time-resolved interrogation of gas-cladding optomechanical dynamics in an anti-resonant hollow-core fiber. The resulting photoacoustic response encodes molecular absorption into the acoustic amplitude, while the resonance frequency and linewidth of the acoustic modes reveal mechanical properties. These results establish a versatile platform for time-resolved optomechanical spectroscopy in microstructured photonic devices, enabling simultaneous chemical sensing and dynamic mechanical characterization. candidates.abstract: Overcoming a robust host immunity at initial infection sites is the prerequisite of pathogen invasion. For vector-borne pathogens, vector saliva is known to inhibit immune responses at the bite site, which supports the concept of vector-microbe synergy to facilitate pathogen transmission. The causative agent of Lyme disease, Borrelia burgdorferi (Bb), invades hosts through blood feeding by Ixodes ticks. This process is multimodal, requiring naïve larvae feeding simultaneously with physically close Bb-infected nymphs or subsequently to Bb-persistent hosts. Bb produces an outer surface protein, CspZ, binding to complement factor H (FH), a negative regulator of the alternative complement pathway (AP). We found CspZ-Salp20 collaboratively conferring multimodal Bb transmission by promoting AP inactivation and bite site infection. We also observed CspZ and Salp20 to collaboratively reduce Bb-triggered bite site inflammations by transcriptomics. We attribute this collaborative immunomodulation to the natural selection of Salp20 loop and the CspZ FH-binding pocket. These findings thus tested the concept of vector-pathogen synergy, providing candidate targets for transmission-disrupting public health interventions. Here, the authors show that CspZ and Salp20 synergistically confer co-feeding- and dissemination-mediated transmission, and lead to alternative complement pathway inactivation and skin immunomodulation at tick bite sites.

candidates.abstract: The formation of fluid cavities in ovarian follicles is critical for mammalian reproduction, yet its mechanism and functions remain poorly understood. Here, we showed that the interstitial fluid in secondary follicles forms an interconnected network near the oocyte in a dynamically critical regime, facilitating chemical transport across the follicle. Transitioning into tertiary follicles, we observed the emergence of cell death and stably growing fluid cavities, resembling phase separation. Using a binary fluid model, we revealed that a gradient of intercellular tension, as observed experimentally, is sufficient to robustly maintain the dynamically critical regime through the competition between fluid coalescence near the oocyte and percolation throughout the follicle. Perturbing N-cadherin led to fragmentation of fluid network, attenuated oocyte-granulosa cell signalling, and impaired oocyte growth. Together, these findings demonstrate that cell junction mechanics regulate follicular fluid configuration and its regime transition to support functional follicle growth. Dynamic fluid network promotes granulosa cell-oocyte metabolic crosstalk, thereby supporting oocyte maturation and follicle development.

Here, we report crystal structures of TKS in complex with mono-, di-, tri-, and tetraketide intermediates that reflect relevant catalytic states in substrate loading, chain elongation, and cyclization. Recapture-versus-release of the tetraketide intermediate determines whether linear or cyclized products are formed. These findings establish a framework for engineering TKS variants with improved OA production and advance chemoenzymatic methods for producing cannabinoids and structurally diverse polyketides.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Mid-infrared photonics is important for gas monitoring, non-invasive medical diagnostics, and free-space optical links. Realizing high-density photonic integrated circuits in the short-wave mid-infrared (SW-MIR, 2–3 μm) requires compact, efficient microscale lasers that can be integrated on standard platforms. Conventional quantum-well microcavity lasers cannot sustain efficient operation as cavities shrink because lateral carrier diffusion and surface recombination impose a fundamental limit on the threshold, while Auger recombination and thermal carrier leakage losses severely compromise thermal stability in the SW-MIR window. Here, we demonstrate that the strong carrier localization in self-assembled InAs quantum-dot (QD) gain medium circumvents these limitations. A five-stack InAs/InP QD active region achieves room-temperature continuous-wave single-mode lasing in a suspended 5.5 µm microdisk at 2.064 µm. The device also sustains lasing up to 110 °C under pulsed excitation. Temperature-dependent spectra and electronic structure analysis reveal ground-to-excited state dynamics and suppression of thermal carrier leakage. These results demonstrate the potential of QD gain media for compact SW-MIR light sources on InP and Si photonic platforms.

candidates.title: Evolution tunes functional sub-state interconversion to boost enzyme function
candidates.authors: Daniel Salamonsen, Andrea Pierangelini, Karol Buda, Daojiong Wang, Felix Schwab, Marc W. van der Kamp, Nobuhiko Tokuriki, H. Adrian Bunzel, Christopher Frøhlich
candidates.abstract: Abstract Enzymes do not operate as static structures, but continuously sample an ensemble of conformational sub-states with distinct catalytic activities. Yet whether evolution can exploit the transitions between sub-states to improve activity remains largely unexplored. Here, we dissect an evolutionary trajectory of β-lactamase OXA-48 toward enhanced ceftazidime hydrolysis. OXA-48 is well suited for studying sub-state evolution, as equilibria between sub-states can be directly interrogated through substrate-induced inactivation and binding kinetics. Steady-state and pre-steady-state kinetic analyses reveal that evolution perturbed the conformational equilibrium and gradually shifted the rate-limiting step from substrate binding through sub-state interconversion to the chemical step. Kinetics with the native substrate meropenem, confirmed coexisting sub-states with markedly different reactivity to ceftazidime, demonstrating that remodeling the conformational landscape introduced a catalytic trade-off rooted in an incompatibility between the native and evolved sub-state populations. Hydrogen/deuterium exchange mass spectrometry independently corroborated these coexisting sub-states, while molecular dynamics simulations traced the activity trade-off to increased active-site flexibility around the catalytic base. Together, our findings establish sub-state interconversion as a direct target of evolutionary selection, shaping functional divergence and offering distinct strategies for enzyme engineering and drug design.

candidates.authors: Xia Chen, Xiao Yao, Xinxin Yin, Zengcai V. Guo
candidates.abstract: Task rules critically shape how neural populations encode information and generalize across cognitive demands, yet the mechanisms linking rule structure, neural dynamics, and behavior remain poorly understood. Here we investigate how rule congruence modulates neural-ensemble compositionality, geometry and cross-task generalizability in mouse anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). Male mice switched between tactile and auditory delayed-response tasks with aligned (congruent) or conflicting (incongruent) sensory-motor contingencies. Recording from 11,000 ALM neurons revealed rule-dependent compositional coding of stimulus, choice, and outcome. In contrast to congruent switching, incongruent rules reduced cross-task generalizability of these representations, expanded population dimensionality, increased reliance on nonlinear mixed-selectivity, and produced more complex coding geometry. These neural changes paralleled behavioral costs during task transitions. Moreover, congruence-dependent reconfiguration of sensory-choice subspaces in ALM predicted differences in transition costs, implicating ALM in resolving conflicting contingencies. Together, these results show that task congruence regulates neural coding geometry and population dynamics, linking rule-switching complexity to dimensionality of neural resource allocation and cognitive flexibility. How neural populations dynamically reconfigure across tasks is not fully understood. Here authors show that task-rule similarity shapes neural coding and geometry in mouse frontal cortex. Conflicting rules increase dimensionality, reduce cross-task generalization and reshape coding geometry in ways that predict task-switching costs.

Using in vitro and cellular approaches, we show that the chromatin remodeler SMARCAD1, which associates with active replication forks, resolves R-loops near nascen

_ai_assessment.reason: The primary contribution is a molecular-biology finding about DNA replication, chromatin remodeling, and R-loop resolution, not condensed-matter physics.
